title: Trading Human Curation for Synthetic Augmentation in RLVR

paper.title: Trading Human Curation for Synthetic Augmentation in RLVR
paper.abstract: Abstract The supply of high-quality training tasks is a central bottleneck for reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) on agentic language models. Each task requires a sandboxed setup, a prompt, and a hand-authored reward function, and only tasks that pass a quality bar produce useful training signal. Hand-curation at this quality bar does not scale economically to the task counts effective RL training requires, and the substitution rate between automatically generated task variants and human-authored ones is not yet established. We investigate using pre-specified, gate-filtered augmentations of a small hand-authored base as a substitute for additional human curation during RLVR. We formalize the cost-adjusted trade rate ρ cost \rho_{\text{cost}} between augmented and human-authored tasks, measure it through a controlled ablation across training corpora with varying augmentation share, and characterize the end-to-end economics of the augmentation pipeline. Substituting augmented content for additional human-authored tasks retains aggregate held-out generalization on a ten-benchmark suite spanning code, instruction following, reasoning, and multi-turn agentic function-calling. The cost-adjusted trade rate ρ cost \rho_{\text{cost}} between gated synthetic and human-authored RLVR tasks stays in [ 1.4 × , 11.6 × ] [1.4\times,11.6\times] across the plausible c human / c aug c_{\text{human}}/c_{\text{aug}} range.

Whiting Affiliation: Pareto AI Email: mark@pareto.ai Abstract The supply of high-quality training tasks is a central bottleneck for reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) on agentic language models. Each task requires a sandboxed setup, a prompt, and a hand-authored reward function, and only tasks that pass a quality bar produce useful training signal. Hand-curation at this quality bar does not scale economically to the task counts effective RL training requires, and the substitution rate between automatically generated task variants and human-authored ones is not yet established. We investigate using pre-specified, gate-filtered augmentations of a small hand-authored base as a substitute for additional human curation during RLVR. We formalize the cost-adjusted trade rate ρ cost \rho_{\text{cost}} between augmented and human-authored tasks, measure it through a controlled ablation across training corpora with varying augmentation share, and characterize the end-to-end economics of the augmentation pipeline. Substituting augmented content for additional human-authored tasks retains aggregate held-out generalization on a ten-benchmark suite spanning code, instruction following, reasoning, and multi-turn agentic function-calling. The cost-adjusted trade rate ρ cost \rho_{\text{cost}} between gated synthetic and human-authored RLVR tasks stays in [ 1.4 × , 11.6 × ] [1.4\times,11.6\times] across the plausible c human / c aug c_{\text{human}}/c_{\text{aug}} range. 1 Introduction Hand-authoring a single agentic RLVR training task costs hours of expert time: a Docker environment, setup scripts, a natural-language prompt, and a task-defined reward function, plus quality-assurance overhead before the task clears a learnable-zone gate. Only tasks that pass that gate (verifier correctness, learnable-zone solvability, distinctness, faithfulness) produce useful training signal, so the effective supply of high-quality training tasks is the bottleneck reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) on agentic language models actually runs against. At the scale required for effective RLVR training (hundreds to thousands of tasks), human curation alone is economically impractical. Prior work scaling RL training data has defaulted to expanding human curation, with OpenAssistant [ 25 ] collecting 161k human dialogue annotations, Tülu 3 [ 26 ] relying on extensive human-curated post-training mixes, and SWE-Gym [ 27 ] hand-curating agentic GitHub-based environments. Prior synthetic-data work in this setting [ 4 , 1 ] has not established the cost-quality limit for augmentation, leaving expanded human curation as the de facto scaling route. To test whether synthetic task variants can substitute for additional human curation, we run a controlled ablation that measures the trade rate ρ \rho , the ratio of marginal pass@1 gain per augmented task to marginal pass@1 gain per human task. Together with a cost ratio c human / c aug c_{\text{human}}/c_{\text{aug}} , ρ \rho determines whether augmentation dominates human curation as a scaling strategy. The four primary arms follow the naming convention H h h _A a a with h h hand-authored tasks and a a augmented variants. H10_A0 and H97_A0 are human-only. H10_A80 (10 base + + 80 augmented) is near-step-matched to H97_A0, and H10_A319 (10 base + + 319 augmented) is the cost-advantaged scaled augmented arm (cheaper than H97_A0 across the swept c human / c aug c_{\text{human}}/c_{\text{aug}} range). We additionally train two compute-matched extended arms, H97_A0 † and H10_A80 † , to the H10_A319 total step count under the same configuration, isolating task source from training-compute confounds. All other GRPO hyperparameters, model (Qwen3.5-27B), evaluation schedule, and held-out suite are held fixed across arms. From a 10-task hand-authored base, 80 gated augmented variants reach the held-out generalization band of 97 fully hand-authored tasks on a ten-benchmark suite spanning code, instruction following, reasoning, knowledge, and multi-turn agentic tool use (grand-mean within 0.20 0.20 percentage points of the human-only baseline, Figure 1 ). At cost-equivalent scale, 319 augmented variants are directionally better than the 97-task human-only baseline by + 0.96 +0.96 percentage points on the aggregate, with 8 of 10 per-benchmark wins. The cost-adjusted trade rate ρ cost \rho_{\text{cost}} between gated synthetic and human-authored RLVR tasks stays in [ 1.4 × , 11.6 × ] [1.4\times,11.6\times] across the plausible c human / c aug c_{\text{human}}/c_{\text{aug}} range. Figure 1: Data-curation cost ( x x , log scale relative to H10_A0 baseline) versus ten-benchmark grand-mean pass@1 ( y y ). Shaded horizontal bands for the augmented arms span the swept c human / c aug ∈ [ 5 × , 42 × ] c_{\text{human}}/c_{\text{aug}}\in[5\times,42\times] range (OpenAssistant low end to SWE-Gym high end). Augmented arms reach H97_A0 quality at lower data-curation cost across the entire sweep: H10_A80 matches H97_A0 within 0.20 0.20 percentage points; H10_A319 sits directionally above by + 0.96 +0.96 percentage points (within propagated aggregate standard error). H10_A0 and H97_A0 cost positions are exact (per-task cost cancels in the ratio); aug arms are bands because the trade rate ρ cost \rho_{\text{cost}} depends on the human/aug per-task cost ratio. Error bars: propagated decoding-seed standard deviation. Our primary contribution is a pilot, single-training-seed result (three decoding seeds per held-out cell). The data are consistent with pre-specified, gate-filtered augmentation of a small hand-authored base substituting for additional human curation in agentic RLVR at lower data-curation cost, under a stated practical-equivalence margin (§ 6.3 ) and the swept c human / c aug c_{\text{human}}/c_{\text{aug}} range (§ 6.2 ). We: • formalize the cost-adjusted trade rate ρ cost \rho_{\text{cost}} between synthetic and human-authored RLVR tasks and measure it end-to-end against matched compute- and cost-equivalent human baselines (§ 4 , § 6.1 ); • show that high-share augmentation reaches the held-out generalization band of additional human curation on a ten-benchmark held-out suite (H10_A80 grand-mean within 0.20 0.20 percentage points of H97_A0; H10_A319 directionally better at + 0.96 +0.96 percentage points, 8 of 10 per-benchmark wins), at ρ cost ∈ [ 1.4 × , 11.6 × ] \rho_{\text{cost}}\in[1.4\times,11.6\times] across the plausible c human / c aug c_{\text{human}}/c_{\text{aug}} range (§ 6.3 , Figure 1 ); • characterize the pipeline calibration regime, with 25.5 % 25.5\% gate yield and a dominant 64 % 64\% too_easy rejection mode that identifies planner overshoot toward easy variants as the next calibration target (§ 6.2 ). 2 Related Work 2.1 Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) Yue et al. [ 7 ] argue that RLVR gains come from sampling efficiency on already-solvable problems rather than capability expansion, with pass@1 improving while pass@ k k at large k k does not exceed the base model. Verifier reliability is also a known concern. TinyV [ 9 ] reports false-negative rates up to 38% on rule-based verifiers. Agentic-RLVR scaling has been demonstrated at the algorithm and model-size axes, with Agent-RLVR [ 1 ] lifting SWE-bench from 9.4% to 22.4% on a 72B model, DeepSeek-R1-Zero [ 2 ] showing reasoning emergence via pure RL without SFT, and Med-RLVR [ 3 ] reporting + 8 +8 percentage points out-of-distribution gains on a 3B base. We respond to verifier reliability with a multiplicative quality gate (Section 3.2 ) and hybrid verification (§ D ). Orthogonal to these works, our contribution targets the task generation axis of agentic RLVR, not the algorithm or model size. 2.2 Synthetic Task Augmentation for RL Data augmentation is well-established in supervised learning but underexplored for RL training environments. In vision-based RL, image augmentations (crop, shift, color jitter) improve sample efficiency [ 21 , 22 ] . For language tasks, paraphrasing and backtranslation provide surface diversity without altering the underlying task. Curriculum methods [ 23 , 24 ] select or generate tasks at the frontier of agent competence. Closest to our work, ReSyn [ 4 ] reports + 27 % +27\% on BBEH via synthetic task augmentation, AgentRL [ 5 ] achieves SOTA on ALFWorld/WebShop/DB with multi-turn multi-task RL, and ProRL Agent [ 6 ] validates the rollout-as-a-service pattern for agentic RL. Neither ReSyn nor AgentRL formalizes a substitution rate between synthetic and human-authored tasks or reports end-to-end pipeline cost (acceptance yield, per-axis variance, per-variant dollar cost). Both demonstrate that augmentation helps without quantifying how much it substitutes per dollar. We expand the pool of training tasks through a pre-specified mutation pipeline that changes what the task requires the agent to do (gated by automated quality filters within the learnable zone pass@8 ∈ [ 0.05 , 0.95 ] \in[0.05,0.95] ) and measure the resulting per-dollar substitution rate end-to-end against matched compute- and cost-equivalent human baselines. 2.3 Cost-Quality Trade-offs in AI Systems Recent work frames AI system design as a cost-quality trade-off problem. Hybrid-LLM routing [ 19 ] routes 22 % 22\% of queries to a cheaper model with < < 1 % 1\% quality drop, crowdsourcing-with-error-correction [ 18 ] achieves 10 × 10\times throughput at controlled error rates, and reasoning-token budgeting [ 20 ] compresses without proportional performance loss. We apply the same lens to training data , treating human tasks as the expensive, high-quality option and augmented tasks as the cheap, potentially-lower-quality option, with the trade rate ρ \rho quantifying training signal lost per dollar saved. 3 Methodology 3.1 Augmentation Pipeline For each base task we (i) generate a scout variant that probes task-specific constraints, then (ii) fan out remaining variants in parallel using pre-specified deterministic mutation strategies (information removal, constraint densification, reference vaguification; full enumeration in § B ), following the seed-task-fan-out tradition of Self-Instruct [ 28 ] and the directed-mutation tradition of Evol-Instruct [ 29 ] . Both the augmentation engine and the agentic component of the task-defined reward function are implemented with a frontier model (Claude Opus 4.6, accessed via API; the same model fills both roles in this study). Reproducibility implications of this closed-weight dependency are discussed in § A . Each variant is then passed through the quality gate (Section 3.2 ). Diversity steering prevents sibling redundancy across the variant pool (§ C ). Figure 2 traces the full variant lifecycle from base task through gate decision. 10 base tasks Scout variant Mutation strategies Diversity steering Gate Q ≥ 0.5 Q\!\geq\!0.5 Accepted variant Reject 74.5% (64% too_easy ) Figure 2: Augmentation-pipeline lifecycle. Each base task expands through a scout variant, parallel pre-specified mutation strategies, and diversity steering (domain + failure-mode axes). Variants pass through the multiplicative quality gate Q = V verify × V solve × V distinct × V faithful × V informative Q=V_{\text{verify}}\!\times\!V_{\text{solve}}\!\times\!V_{\text{distinct}}\!\times\!V_{\text{faithful}}\!\times\!V_{\text{informative}} at threshold 0.5.
